Saint Augustine repeatedly touched on the problem of marriage, sometimes in passing in many of his works, and other times, more of substance and purpose, as in his luminous treatises On adulterous liaisons, On marriage and concupiscence, On the good of marriage, in epistles 200, 262, 137 and 150 and in some of his sermons, such as 9, On the ten strings, in which he brings his Rebuke. to adulterers, and 51, Concordia between Saint Matthew and Saint Luke on the generation of the Lord, in which we find his famous passage that deals with how marriage does not consist in the mixing of the flesh.
The treatise On the Good of Marriage, in a single book, was composed by the Saint in the year 401, followed, as a complement and clarification of this, by the book of Holy Virginity.

Saint Augustine, undefeated polemicist, attentive to combating every shadow of error that could undermine the integrity and luster of Christian dogmatics and morals, felt compelled to quell at its roots every outbreak of heresy that disturbed the beliefs and practices of his flock. And what he wrote for his Hyponian flock soon crossed African limits and was joyfully accepted by all the churches and episcopates of the Catholic world, of which Augustine was the greatest luminary.

This treatise On the Good of Marriage, which now appears for the first time in a Spanish version, was written by the Saint to refute the attacks against virginity of a certain monk called Joviniano. The natural complement of this book is On Holy Virginity, in which he makes his apology and sings of his excellences,

In the book On Marriage and Concupiscence, Saint Augustine alludes to the Jovinian heresy. "Jovinian," says the Saint in chapter 23, "who a few years ago attempted to institute a new heresy, maintained that the Catholics supported the Manichaeans, because contrary to their opinion, like them, they put holy virginity before marriage."

In this beautiful treatise Saint Augustine speaks, with his demon. usual acuity and with its discursive force, about marriage. He demonstrates with inconclusive reasoning that marriage is a good, and not a relative good in comparison with fornication, but a good in its kind, in itself. Consequently, there is no shadow of sin in the holy sacrament of marriage, although in its use there may be excesses and incontinences that do not exempt from some sin.

However, although marriage is good and holy, the Holy One judges that contineacy is much higher and more excellent. He believes that the marriage of the patriarchs was better than the continence of those who are restrained today, because it was necessary for the propagation of the species and for the promised Redeemer to be born from them. They, however, te-. They had habitual continence, and thus they united in themselves the virtue of marriage and the virtue of conjugal continence.

Now, the Saint judges that, since in the Gospel it is said when speaking of continence: he who can understand, let him understand, only those who cannot contain themselves in chastity should go to marriage. It is clear that since these must always be in small numbers, there is no danger to the spread and conservation of the human race.

He warmly defends the marriage of the holy patriarchs even over the continence of those who today live in chastity, because they united, to the obedience of marriage, the habitual desire for a desired continence.

Against those who defended marriage against virginity, the Saint gathers reasons, subtleties, and eloquence to demonstrate that both marriage and contineaty or virginity are two positive goods, although one is superior to the other.

The language of the Saint is expressive and strong. He doesn't go around with euphemisms or distortions. Call things by their name. So much so that today, although it is not a time of honesty or modesty in deeds or words, it is possible that the words of the Saint seem excessively clear and harsh to many ears accustomed to the hypocrisy of a fictitious modesty in words when impudence and scandal in actions, in a relaxed and clumsy life, are neither feared nor avoided. And we have often tried to mitigate the graphic expressions of the Saint.

Santiago Pame- * Mo believed he found a contradiction between this booklet and canon 104 of the IV Carthaginian Council, which establishes that widows consecrated to God be excommunicated and treated as adulteresses if they remarry. Saint Augustine attended that council and subscribed to the canons. But there is no such contradiction. The widow consecrated to God is equated to the consecrated virgin. If she broke her vow she was considered an adulteress, and perhaps that created some difficulties in this matter, as can be seen in this same booklet. Augustine says with the council that they should be treated like adulteresses, but he says here on his own that there is no adultery strictly speaking, although there is perhaps a greater sin than adultery, a sacrilege. Located between Maniguesm and Pelagianism, Agustin masterfully handles the helm, defending the theoretical points with serenity, skillfully insinuating himself to inspire desires for heroic virtue, not only to those who consult him, but to all those who come before him in his preparation, and responding to occasional difficulties.

When Bishop Polente read a treatise by Saint Augustine on the Sermon on the Mount, he found some difficulties about marriage and its indissolubility in the doctrine of the Gospels and in Saint Paul, and he honestly sent his objections to the same author of that treatise. Later he made some additions, which Agustín studied again. Here is the theme of these two little books. The courage with which Saint Augustine opposes divorce and maintains the moral and legal equality of men vis-à-vis women gives impressive relevance to these tracts, written around 419.

In contrast to the beloved Pauline privilege, Augustine rather tends to limit as much as possible the cases of separation due to faith, considering that it is much better for the faithful spouse to save the unfaithful and establishing that, in any case, a new marriage is not contracted. The Church has been more benign in interpreting this Pauline privilege, considering it as a case, although exceptional, of the indissolubility of marriage and allowing the faithful spouse to contract new marriages after the unfaithful spouse enters into cohabitation. While Saint Augustine believed that the Apostle promulgated this privilege under his personal and apostolic responsibility, as a license or permission that he granted in his own name, modern Catholic authors consider that the privilege is of divine right or at least

. us of general apostolic law. Because only he who instituted marriage can repeal a marriage contract. In any case, it is not an obligation, but a right granted to the faithful spouse when the unfaithful person refuses to cohabit with him for having accepted the Christian faith,

Against the authenticity of this pamphlet, Erasmus wanted to allege reasons of style, doctrine and omission in the Retractions. But, on the contrary, this type of rhymed prose, with its rhythm and assonant cadences, characterizes African literature very well, and especially Saint Augustine. As for the doctrines, not only do they not differ in any way from those currently presented by Saint Augustine, but in this booklet the reader will find the foundations of Augustinian morality, which is at the front of this volume. This booklet is a little piece of research, an almost groping search in this naive and tangled problem. of the lie. Today, when we have a lot of Anconcusan truths, almost untouchable, we cannot give ourselves a clear idea of ​​the effort of those men, who, Pugilists, were building, premise by premise, the system of our beliefs. When Saint Augustine undertook this discussion, some Catholics denied that lying was licit, authorizing themselves to do so from some passages of the Sacred Scripture *. And Agustin has to start finding out. The booklet is conclusive due to its illicitness, but his thought will not be fully elucidated until he writes another work twenty-five years later, which he will dedicate to a Spanish monk, Consencio: Contra Mendactum (Against Lies.

The present De mendacio (On lying) was written at the beginning of the year 395, a year before his episcopal consecration. And about it he tells us in the Retractions (1,27): «I also wrote a book On Lies, which, although difficult to read, is, however, very useful as an exercise of wit and intelligence and greatly stimulates the love of truthfulness. I had ordered it removed from among my pamphlets because it seemed dark, thorny and extremely difficult to me, which is why I had not even managed to publish it. After having written the other pamphlet entitled Against Lies, I was more confirmed in the decision to destroy it, and so I ordered it; but it was not done. When reviewing all my pamphlets now, I have found it Incolume and, after correcting it, I have ordered it to be preserved, especially because it has some necessary notes that are not found in the other. Furthermore, that one is titled Against Lies, and this On Lies, already indicating in the title that the former is an open attack against lies, while the latter is above all an essay of discussion and search. Both tend, however, to the same end. This book begins: "This lie is a serious problem..."

INTRODUCTION TO THE "SERMON OF THE MONIAÑAD m INTRODUCTION Some years later, leafing through this treatise of Saint Augustine, a certain Polenclos, came across some difficulties about the woman who separated from her husband, and he proposed them to the holy Doctor. This forced him to return to these books of his Youth and helped him to complete his thoughts and resolve the doubts of his communicator, writing the book De coniuglis adulterinis and the appropriate annotations in book 1, chapter 19, of the Retractations. Consequently, in the first years after the Saint demonstrated the profound assimilation of the spirit of his conversion, Saint Augustine wrote his exposition of Christian Being, the richness of thought, the clarity and gallantry of the Monta. It is the fruit, without a doubt, of his first days of exposition. d meditations and catechism to the Christian people. The Saint, master of the most well-known works, would later return to this evangelical subject and would expand his thoughts in sermons, commentaries and exegesis. Sermon on the Mount is inexhaustible. It is logical that he requested corresponding Tes. the attention of the Saint, always zealous to indoctrinate and guide the faithful with the word and spirit of the Holy Scriptures, Saint Augustine composed this treatise—which is an exegesis between doctrinal and catechetical—De Sermone Domani in Monte between the years 393-394, being—as already indicated—only a presbyter. This is what the Saint implies in the first Mbro De Retractationibus, where, after having reviewed the dispute that he had about the Symbol of Faith in the council of Hippo, in the year 393, he speaks of his imperfect work De Genesi ad litteram, without indicating any other date than that of the aforementioned council, and immediately mentions this work with the following words: <At the same time I wrote two books explaining the sermon of the Lord on the mount, according to Saint Matthew.» In the first of these books he exposes the first part contained in chapter 5 of the Gospel of Saint Matthew, and in the second book, the remainder of the sermon, which includes chapters 6 and 7.

The Saint carefully analyzes the beatitudes, following the letter of Saint Matthew throughout the first book and part of the second, until reaching chapter 4, in which the exposition of the sermon is interrupted, in a clear way to begin the explanation, certainly luminous and sagacious, of the Lord's Prayer, studying the petitions one by one and clarifying with sharp interpretations the words and meaning of the Sunday prayer. In chapter 12 of book 2, Saint Augustine resumes his exposition of the beatitudes, and expands on precious considerations about trust in God, Providence, fasting, reckless julelos, perseverance in prayer, false prophets, the meaning and use of temporal blessings, etc.
